opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that Project GR00T is really a full-stack effort. It's not just a single model. When people hear "foundation model for humanoid robots," they tend to picture one big neural network, but the model is only one piece of a much broader pipeline we need to build.

I like to break it down into three computers, which is how NVIDIA frames it too. First, there's the computer for training the model, the big data center GPUs where we train the foundation model itself. Second, there's the simulation computer, which is where Omniverse and Isaac Sim come in. That's where we generate huge amounts of synthetic data and let robots practice in physically accurate virtual worlds, much faster than real time. Third, there's the computer that runs on the robot, the edge compute like Jetson Thor, which has to run these models efficiently in real time on the humanoid itself.

On the data side, I think about it as a pyramid. At the top you have real robot data, collected through teleoperation. It's the highest quality and the most relevant, but it's very expensive and doesn't scale, because you're limited by the number of robots and human hours. In the middle you have simulation data, which you can scale with compute instead of human labor. You can take a handful of human demonstrations and multiply them, with different environments, lighting, object positions, and physics parameters. At the bottom, the broadest layer, is internet-scale data, mainly videos of humans doing things. It doesn't come with action labels, but it carries a huge amount of prior knowledge about how the world works and how people interact with objects.

So the breadth of the pipeline comes from needing to stitch all of these together: the data strategy across real, sim, and internet; the training infrastructure; the simulation tooling; and the deployment hardware. Our job at NVIDIA is to provide that whole platform so humanoid companies don't have to rebuild everything from scratch. They can bring their own robot body and plug into the stack.

I think that breadth is necessary because robotics doesn't have its own "internet of actions" the way language models had the web. We have to manufacture that data, and doing it well takes the whole pipeline working together.

r001.rationale: The response says humanoid companies can bring their own robot body and use the stack, but it does not state that the pipeline adapts to robot platforms beyond humanoids.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the robot foundation model is only as good as the data and the infrastructure you can feed it, and in robotics, unlike language, you can't just scrape the internet. So we had to build the whole stack ourselves, and that's why it looks so broad.

I usually describe it as a pyramid. At the bottom you have internet-scale data, human videos, the kind of thing that teaches a model what a kitchen looks like, how hands manipulate objects, the priors about the physical world. That's abundant but it's not robot-actionable. Above that you have simulation, which is where NVIDIA has a real advantage. With Isaac, Omniverse, and now generative world models, we can produce enormous amounts of physically grounded data with action labels, and we can randomize environments, lighting, textures, physics parameters, to a degree that's simply impossible in the real world. And at the top of the pyramid you have real robot data, teleoperation, which is the most precious and the most expensive. A human has to put on a headset and move a humanoid around for hours.

So the pipeline exists to connect those layers. We have tools for collecting teleop data, tools for taking a small number of human demonstrations and multiplying them in simulation by orders of magnitude, tools for generating synthetic trajectories, and then the training recipes that blend all of it into a single model like GR00T N1. The breadth isn't because we like building tools. It's because every missing piece becomes the bottleneck. If you have a great simulator but no way to turn ten demos into ten thousand, you're stuck. If you have great data but the model can't transfer from sim to real, you're stuck.

The other principle is that we try to build it as a platform rather than a single bespoke pipeline. Humanoids from different companies, different hands, different sensors, they all need to plug in. So the tools have to be general enough that a partner can bring their embodiment and their data and still benefit from the foundation model. That's the bet. Language models became powerful because the whole ecosystem converged on shared infrastructure, and we want robotics to get its own version of that moment.

r001.rationale: The response says the tools should support humanoids from different companies and embodiments, but it does not state that the pipeline adapts to platforms beyond humanoids.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as an entire pipeline, because a robot foundation model by itself isn’t enough. You need a way to collect data, a way to train the model, a way to evaluate it, and then a way to deploy it on a physical robot and learn from what happens.

The data part is especially interesting. With language, you have the internet. With robotics, you don’t have that same abundance of examples of actions and their consequences. So you need multiple ways to generate experience: human demonstrations, simulation, and interaction with the real world. And you need tools that let those sources reinforce each other.

That’s how I think about the breadth of Project Groot. The goal is a generalist robot, but getting there means building the infrastructure around the model, too. You want a loop where better data improves the policy, evaluation reveals what it’s missing, and those failures guide the next round of data collection.

r001.rationale: The response describes a broad pipeline for building a generalist robot, but it does not say the pipeline can adapt to robot platforms beyond humanoids.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as building an entire ecosystem, because a robot foundation model is only one piece of the puzzle. You need a way to collect demonstrations, a way to turn those demonstrations into much more diverse training data, a simulator where robots can practice, and then the infrastructure to train and deploy the model on real hardware.

The data piece is especially important. With language, you have the internet. With robotics, you don’t have an internet of physical interactions that you can just download. So you have to build that pipeline: collect human demonstrations, augment them in simulation, vary the objects and environments, and use those experiences to improve the policy.

And all of those pieces have to work together. Where does the robot fail? Can we reproduce that failure in simulation? Can we generate more examples and bring the improved policy back to the robot? That feedback loop is how I think about the breadth of GR00T. The goal is to make developing robot intelligence a repeatable process that can scale across tasks and different robot bodies.

r001.rationale: The response says the process can scale across “different robot bodies,” but does not clearly state that it adapts to platforms beyond humanoids; different bodies could still mean different humanoid platforms.
